en: To become less intense or widespread; to decrease
hook: ABATE: the storm takes A BATH and calms down.
story: Abate. All night, Cyclone Sitrang screamed over the coast of Bhola. Tin roofs flew like paper. Palm trees bent to the ground. Families huddled in the concrete shelter, children crying, nobody sleeping. Then, around dawn, the howling slowly softened. By nine, only a steady breeze remained. By noon, birds were singing again. The storm had abated: it had become less intense, little by little. Pain abates, anger abates, floods abate. Think of a storm taking a long, calming bath.

gre.s: The protesters vowed to continue until the government met their demands, so their anger is unlikely to ____ any time soon.
gre.clue: vowed to continue until the government met their demands

en: To formally and solemnly give up a belief, claim, or habit
bn: শপথ করে ত্যাগ করা; প্রকাশ্যে বর্জন করা
hook: AB-JURE: 'ab' is away, 'jure' is swear (jury). To swear it away.
story: Abjure. Kamal had driven drunk for years and always laughed it off. Then one night he crashed into a rickshaw. The puller survived, barely. The next morning, Kamal stood before his whole family, poured every bottle down the drain, and swore on his mother's head never to drink again. Ten years later, he never has. To abjure is to formally and solemnly renounce a belief, habit, or claim. Ab means away, jure means swear: to swear something away.

gre.s: Forced to ____ his heretical views before the tribunal, the astronomer publicly renounced theories he privately continued to hold.
gre.clue: publicly renounced

en: Deviating from what is normal or expected
hook: A-NOMAL-ous: 'a-normal', not normal.
story: Anomalous. Nadia's GRE practice scores were steady: 310, 311, 309, 312. Then one Tuesday she scored 334. She screamed. She called her mother. Then her tutor looked closer and frowned. Nadia had accidentally taken a beginner-level practice test. The 334 was anomalous: it did not fit the pattern at all. Anomalous means deviating from what is normal or expected. In science passages, anomalous data are the strange results that challenge an accepted theory.

gre.s: Because every other sample showed the same chemical signature, researchers dismissed the one ____ reading as the result of contamination.
gre.clue: every other sample showed the same chemical signature

en: A deep-seated feeling of dislike or hostility
hook: ANTI-PATHY: ANTI-feeling, the opposite of sympathy.
story: Antipathy. Thirty years ago, Mr. Rahim and Mr. Karim argued over a mango tree on the boundary between their houses. Nobody remembers who won. But since that day, they have not spoken a single word to each other. They skip each other's weddings, cross the road to avoid each other, and grumble whenever the other's name is mentioned. That is antipathy: a deep, settled dislike or hostility. Anti means against, pathy means feeling. It is the opposite of sympathy.

gre.s: The two philosophers' mutual ____ was well known; each rarely missed a chance to ridicule the other's work in print.
gre.clue: rarely missed a chance to ridicule the other's work

en: Mysterious and known or understood by only a few people
hook: ARCANE: hidden in an ARK, like secret knowledge only priests can read.
story: Arcane. Every Eid, Rafi's grandfather pulls out a worn deck of cards and tries to teach the grandchildren an old village game. It has thirty-two rules, secret signals, and scoring that changes depending on the moon. Nobody under seventy remembers how it works. By the second round, the children always give up. Those rules are arcane: mysterious and understood by only a few people. Arcane knowledge is hidden, like secrets locked in an ark. Tax law often feels arcane.

gre.s: The scholar's knowledge of ____ medieval manuscripts, which perhaps a dozen people in the world could read, made her indispensable to the museum.
gre.clue: which perhaps a dozen people in the world could read

en: Requiring great effort and endurance; very difficult
hook: ARDUOUS sounds like HARD-uous: hard work.
story: Arduous. The trek to Keokradong began at dawn. Six hours of steep climbing. Slippery red mud. Leeches. Burning sun. Twice, Sara sat on a rock and seriously considered turning back. Her legs trembled; her water ran out. But at the top, the hills rolled away in waves of green and silver mist, and every step felt worth it. Arduous means extremely hard and tiring, requiring great effort. Arduous sounds like hard-uous. Preparing for the GRE while working full time is arduous too.

gre.s: After months of ____ negotiations, marked by walkouts and late-night sessions, the two sides finally signed the agreement.
gre.clue: marked by walkouts and late-night sessions

en: Simple, natural, and sincere; without deceit or cunning
hook: ART-LESS: no art of trickery. Natural and honest.
story: Artless. At the dinner party, Auntie served her new chicken recipe and asked everyone what they thought. The adults said, "Delicious!" Then little Joya, aged six, announced, "It is too salty, but the dessert is very nice." Everyone laughed, including Auntie. Joya was not being rude. She simply had no tricks, no pretence, no social games. That is artless: natural, simple, and sincere, without deceit. It is a compliment. Artless means without the art of cunning, not without skill.

gre.s: The child's ____ remarks, free of any calculation or flattery, charmed the guests far more than the polished speeches of the adults.
gre.clue: free of any calculation or flattery

en: Practicing severe self-discipline and avoiding all pleasures, often for religious reasons
hook: ASCETIC sounds like 'a SKEPTIC of pleasure': refuses all comfort.
story: Ascetic. High in the hills of Bandarban lives a monk who owns two robes, one bowl, and nothing else. He sleeps on a straw mat, eats one plain meal before noon, and spends hours in silent meditation. Visitors bring him gifts; he gives them away. He chose this life deliberately. Ascetic means practising strict self-denial, avoiding all pleasure and comfort, often for spiritual reasons. Do not confuse it with aesthetic, which is about beauty. Ascetic sounds like a skeptic of pleasure.

gre.s: Though heir to a vast fortune, the philosopher lived an ____ life, renouncing luxury and subsisting on bread and water.
gre.clue: renouncing luxury and subsisting on bread and water

en: To make an unpleasant feeling less intense; to satisfy a need
hook: ASSUAGE sounds like 'a massage': it soothes the pain.
story: Assuage. The night before her visa interview, Mitu could not breathe properly. What if they ask about money? What if I forget my documents? What if my English fails? At midnight her elder sister called from Toronto. For an hour they practised questions, laughed, and planned. By the end, Mitu's fear had melted into calm. Her sister had assuaged it. To assuage is to ease or soothe a painful feeling, or to satisfy a need. A cold drink assuages thirst. Assuage sounds like a soothing massage.

gre.s: The airline offered free hotel rooms and meals in an attempt to ____ the anger of passengers stranded by the cancellation.
gre.clue: in an attempt to

en: To be disloyal to; also, to unintentionally reveal something
bn: বিশ্বাসঘাতকতা করা; অজান্তে প্রকাশ করে ফেলা
hook: GRE trick: BETRAY often means REVEAL — your trembling hands betray your nerves.
story: Betray. "I am not nervous at all," Tanvir told the interview panel with a confident smile. But as he reached for the glass of water, his hand shook so badly that the water splashed across the table. His trembling hands betrayed him: they revealed exactly the fear he was hiding. On the GRE, betray often means to reveal something unintentionally, not only to be disloyal. A blush can betray embarrassment; an accent can betray where you grew up.

gre.s: Although the novelist insists her characters are invented, certain details ____ an intimate knowledge of her own family's history.
gre.clue: Although the novelist insists her characters are invented

en: Relating to the pleasant aspects of the countryside; rural
hook: BUCOLIC: 'boo-cow-lic', cows mooing in green fields.
story: Bucolic. After five years of Dhaka traffic, Zayan finally visited his grandparents' village in Kurigram. He woke to roosters instead of horns. Cows grazed beside a silver pond. Children fished with bamboo rods, and his grandmother sang while drying rice in the sun. For a week, he forgot his phone existed. It felt like a painting come to life: bucolic. Bucolic means relating to the pleasant, peaceful side of country life. Imagine the gentle boo of cows in a green field.

gre.s: The painter's early landscapes are ____ idylls of shepherds and grazing cattle, a sharp contrast to her later images of crowded industrial cities.
gre.clue: shepherds and grazing cattle

en: To grow or expand rapidly
hook: BURGEON: a BURGER shop that grows into a giant chain overnight.
story: Burgeon. Ten years ago, Farhan's cousin started a tiny online shop selling handmade notebooks from her bedroom. She shipped five orders a week. Then social media found her. Fifty orders a week. Five hundred. Today she runs a warehouse with forty employees. Her business burgeoned: it grew and flourished rapidly, like buds bursting open in spring. Burgeoning populations, burgeoning cities, burgeoning careers. Think of a tiny burger stall that suddenly becomes a nationwide chain.

gre.s: Scientists warn that, unless strict controls are introduced, the city's population will continue to ____, straining already overloaded water supplies.
gre.clue: straining already overloaded water supplies

en: Harsh, loud, and unpleasant-sounding
hook: CACO = bad, PHONE = sound. Bad sound.
story: Cacophonous. At five in the evening, Gulistan intersection becomes a symphony from hell. Bus horns blare. Rickshaw bells jangle. A loudspeaker blasts film songs from one shop while another blasts a sermon. Vendors scream prices. A traffic policeman blows his whistle at no one in particular. Imran covered his ears and laughed. The noise was cacophonous: harsh, jarring, and unpleasant. Caco means bad, phone means sound. Its opposite is euphonious, meaning sweet to hear.

gre.s: The composer deliberately made the opening ____, layering clashing rhythms and harsh brass so that the gentle melody that follows seems all the sweeter.
gre.clue: layering clashing rhythms and harsh brass

en: To officially declare someone a saint; to treat as sacred or beyond criticism
bn: সন্ত বলে ঘোষণা করা; মহিমান্বিত করা
hook: CANONIZE: fired from a CANON of saints, officially added to the holy list.
story: Canonize. In 2016, the church officially declared Mother Teresa a saint, adding her name to its canon, its official list of saints. That is the original meaning of canonize. But the word has grown. When fans treat a celebrity as perfect and beyond criticism, they canonize her. When every literature syllabus includes a novel, that novel has been canonized as a classic. To canonize is to declare sacred, or to treat as beyond question. It is a close cousin of deify.

gre.s: Within a decade of his death, critics who had dismissed the poet began to ____ him, ranking his verse among the greatest of the century.
gre.clue: ranking his verse among the greatest of the century

en: To express severe, formal disapproval
hook: CENSURE: like a CENSOR, it officially condemns what you did.
story: Censure. The minister had told parliament that the new bridge cost fifty crore taka. Then journalists found the real figure: one hundred and twenty crore. The parliament did not remove him from office, but it voted to censure him, a formal, public statement of strong disapproval written into the official record. His career never recovered. To censure is to criticize severely and officially. Do not confuse it with censor, which means to cut or ban content.

gre.s: The medical board voted to ____ the surgeon for his reckless conduct, though it stopped short of revoking his license.
gre.clue: his reckless conduct

en: The use of clever trickery to deceive
hook: CHICANERY: a CHICKEN-sly fox's trick.
story: Chicanery. The company's advertisement promised to double your money in three months. Smiling agents visited villages with glossy brochures and fake testimonials. Retired teachers and farmers handed over their life savings. Then, one Monday, the office was empty and the phones were dead. The founders had flown abroad. The whole scheme had been chicanery: clever trickery used to deceive people, especially in business, law, or politics. Picture a sly fox tricking a chicken out of its eggs.

gre.s: The lawyer's courtroom victories owed less to sound argument than to ____: misleading exhibits, coached witnesses, and procedural tricks.
gre.clue: misleading exhibits, coached witnesses, and procedural tricks

en: To come together and form a single group or mass
bn: একত্রিত হওয়া; মিলিত হয়ে এক হওয়া
hook: CO-ALESCE: COAL pieces fusing together in heat into one lump.
story: Coalesce. At first, the students' complaints were scattered. One group grumbled about fees. Another about the broken library. Another about the terrible canteen food. Nobody listened. Then, over one month of late-night meetings, the separate voices merged into a single movement with one list of demands and one leader. The administration finally paid attention. The complaints had coalesced: come together to form one whole. Raindrops on a window coalesce into one big drop.

gre.s: Over several centuries, the scattered tribes began to ____ into a single kingdom with a shared language and a common law.
gre.clue: into a single kingdom

en: Clear, logical, and convincing
hook: COGENT: every COG in the argument fits perfectly.
story: Cogent. Sara wanted a laptop for her GRE preparation. Instead of begging, she prepared a presentation for her parents: the online courses she needed, a comparison of laptop prices against cyber-café fees over one year, and a plan to repay half of the cost from her tutoring income. Her father put down his tea. "That is a very cogent argument." She got the laptop that weekend. Cogent means clear, logical, and convincing. Every cog fits.

gre.s: The committee found the proposal's reasoning so ____ that even its harshest skeptics conceded they could find no flaw in it.
gre.clue: could find no flaw in it

en: Evoking strong interest or attention; very convincing
hook: COMPELLING: it COMPELS, or forces, you to pay attention.
story: Compelling. Arif told himself, "Just one episode, then sleep." The new detective series opened with a murder on a ferry. Then a twist. Then a cliffhanger. At four in the morning, he was still watching, eyes burning, unable to stop. The story was compelling: so powerfully interesting that it forced him to keep going. Compelling also means convincing: compelling evidence persuades a jury. Either way, a compelling thing compels you, pushing you to pay attention.

gre.s: Although the evidence for the hypothesis was once considered thin, the new fossil discoveries make a ____ case for it.
gre.clue: Although the evidence for the hypothesis was once considered thin

en: To argue or assert something; to struggle against difficulties
bn: দাবি করা; প্রতিদ্বন্দ্বিতা বা মোকাবেলা করা
hook: CONTEND: CONTENDERs fight in a competition; scholars contend in arguments.
story: Contend. In Professor Haque's history class, the students split into two teams. One team contended that the dinosaurs died because of a giant asteroid. The other team contended that volcanoes were to blame. They argued for an hour, each side firmly asserting its view. Contend means to argue or claim something firmly, a common GRE word in passages about scientific debates. It also means to struggle: farmers contend with floods every monsoon. Contenders compete; contentions are claims.

gre.s: Some economists ____ that the recession was caused by excessive regulation, while others argue that deregulation was to blame.
gre.clue: while others argue

en: Abundant; existing in large amounts
hook: COPIOUS: so many COPIES that there's plenty for all.
story: Copious. Ishita took copious notes in every lecture: three colour-coded pens, diagrams in the margins, and summaries at the end of each page. By the end of the semester she had filled five thick notebooks. When exams arrived, the whole class lined up outside her room asking for photocopies. Copious means plentiful, existing in large quantities. Copious tears, copious rain, copious food at a Bangladeshi wedding. Think: so many copies that there is plenty for everyone.

gre.s: Far from being sparse, the explorer's journals are ____, documenting every plant, river, and conversation she encountered.
gre.clue: Far from being sparse

en: Familiar with and at ease in many different countries and cultures
hook: COSMOS = world, POLIS = city. A citizen of the world.
story: Cosmopolitan. Mitu's aunt has lived in London, Tokyo, Nairobi, and Toronto. She speaks four languages, cooks dishes from twelve countries, and has friends on every continent. At a party she moves easily from a Japanese businessman to a Kenyan artist to a Bangladeshi grandmother, at home with everyone. She is truly cosmopolitan: worldly, sophisticated, and comfortable with many cultures. Cosmos means world, polis means city. A citizen of the world.

gre.s: The port's ____ character, shaped by centuries of traders from dozens of nations, contrasted sharply with the insular villages of the interior.
gre.clue: contrasted sharply with the insular villages

en: Polite submission and respect for another's opinion or authority
hook: DEFERENCE: you DEFER, or step aside, out of respect.
story: Deference. In the village meeting, the young men argued loudly about where to build the new well. Then old Headman Abdul Karim raised one hand. Instantly, everyone fell silent. When he spoke, nobody interrupted, even those who disagreed with him. They lowered their eyes and listened. That is deference: polite, respectful submission to someone's judgment or authority. You defer, or step aside, out of respect. Out of deference to her parents, Sara delayed her trip.

gre.s: Out of ____ to the senior surgeon, the young resident kept her doubts to herself, a silence she later regretted.
gre.clue: kept her doubts to herself

en: Lacking a plan, purpose, or enthusiasm; jumping randomly from one thing to another
hook: DESULTORY: like a DESERT wanderer with no map, aimlessly drifting.
story: Desultory. Tanvir sat down to study at eight. Ten minutes of vocabulary. Then a cricket highlight. Then two geometry problems. Then his phone. Then a snack. Then a random article about sharks. At midnight he realized he had learned almost nothing. His study session had been desultory: aimless, jumping randomly from one thing to another with no plan or purpose. A desultory conversation drifts without going anywhere. Desultory effort produces desultory results.

gre.s: His research, once focused and rigorous, became ____ in his later years, as he drifted from topic to topic without completing any project.
gre.clue: drifted from topic to topic without completing any project

en: Shy and lacking in self-confidence
hook: DIFFIDENT is the opposite of CONFIDENT.
story: Diffident. Rahim knew the answer to every question in physics class. But when the teacher asked, he looked at his desk. When she called his name, he spoke so softly that nobody heard. He doubted himself constantly, certain that he would be wrong. In the final exam, he scored the highest in the class. He was diffident: shy and lacking confidence. Diffident is the opposite of confident. The GRE loves this contrast, so remember: dif-fident, the opposite of con-fident.

gre.s: Though brilliant, the young researcher was so ____ that she rarely presented her findings, fearing that colleagues would find fault with them.
gre.clue: fearing that colleagues would find fault with them

en: Slow to act; intended to cause delay
hook: DILATORY: DELAY-tory.
story: Dilatory. Joya needed a simple birth certificate for her passport. The office told her to come back next week. Next week, the officer was on leave. The week after, a form was missing a stamp. Then the printer broke. Four months and seven visits later, she finally received one sheet of paper. The office was famously dilatory: slow to act, causing delay. Dilatory tactics in court are designed to stall a case. Think: delay-tory.

gre.s: Frustrated by the contractor's ____ progress, the city imposed daily fines for every week the project fell behind schedule.
gre.clue: fell behind schedule

en: To use vague or ambiguous language to avoid committing to an answer
hook: EQUI-VOCATE: EQUAL VOICES, saying both yes and no at once.
story: Equivocate. A reporter asked the minister a simple question: "Will fuel prices rise next month?" The minister smiled. "Well, many complex factors are involved. We are carefully monitoring global trends. Of course, the people's welfare is our highest priority." He spoke for three minutes and said nothing at all. He equivocated: used vague, ambiguous language to avoid committing to an answer. Equi means equal, vocate means voice: speaking equally for yes and no at once.

gre.s: Pressed to say whether she supported the bill, the candidate continued to ____, offering answers so qualified that both sides claimed her as an ally.
gre.clue: offering answers so qualified that both sides claimed her

en: To divide into two sharply opposing groups
bn: মেরুকরণ করা; দুই বিপরীত দলে বিভক্ত করা
hook: POLARIZE: pushes people to opposite POLES, north and south.
story: Polarize. During the World Cup, Priya's class split in two. Half the students wore Argentina shirts; half wore Brazil shirts. Lunch tables divided. Friendships cooled. Even the teachers took sides. Nobody, absolutely nobody, stood in the middle. The tournament had polarized the class: split it into two sharply opposing groups, like the north and south poles of a magnet. Political issues often polarize whole countries, leaving no room for moderate voices.

gre.s: Rather than unite the party, the leader's divisive speech threatened to ____ its members into two hostile camps.
gre.clue: into two hostile camps

en: Spending money or resources recklessly and wastefully
hook: PRODIGAL son: the son in the parable who wasted his whole inheritance.
story: Prodigal. In the famous story, a young man asked his father for his share of the inheritance, travelled to a distant city, and spent every coin on parties, fine clothes, and gambling. Within a year, he was starving, feeding pigs to survive. He walked home in rags, expecting rejection, but his father ran to embrace him. That is the prodigal son. Prodigal means recklessly wasteful with money or resources. Do not confuse it with prodigy, a gifted child.

gre.s: The government's ____ spending during the boom years left it with no reserves when the recession arrived.
gre.clue: left it with no reserves

en: Using more words than needed; wordy
hook: VERBOSE: too many VERBS, too many words.
story: Verbose. The assignment said three hundred words. Arif submitted nine hundred. Instead of "The plan failed," he had written, "The aforementioned plan, unfortunately and regrettably, did not, in the final analysis, ultimately succeed in achieving its intended objectives." His teacher drew a red line through half the page and wrote one comment: "Too verbose. Cut it." Verbose means using far more words than needed. Good GRE essays are concise. Synonyms: wordy, prolix, long-winded.

gre.s: The editor trimmed the manuscript by half, arguing that the author's ____ style buried his best insights under paragraphs of needless elaboration.
gre.clue: paragraphs of needless elaboration
